title: Why the word keeps changing
goal: Face head-on the pattern that makes more beginners give up than any other: one word that shows up in two different shapes. After this unit it stops feeling random.
bekal: recognize the ten most common consonant gradation patterns
memorize nouns as **pairs**, not as a single form
name places in town and say you are there

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Vanalinnas jalutades
dialogs.intro: Budi and Kerli are walking through the Old Town. Budi points at two signs that confuse him.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kerli, ma ei saa aru. Siin on kirjas "pood", aga seal "poe".
lines.id: Kerli, I don't get it. Here it says "pood", but over there "poe".
lines.literal: Kerli, I not can-I understand. here is writing-in "shop", but there "shop-GEN".

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Aa, see on astmevaheldus. Üks sõna, kaks kuju.
lines.id: Ah, that's grade alternation. One word, two shapes.
lines.literal: ah, that is-it grade-alternation. one word, two shape.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.id: "Pood" is the basic form. "Poe" is the genitive — "of the shop".
lines.literal: "shop" is-it basic-shape. "shop-GEN" is-it genitive — "of the shop".

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And do all words do that?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How do I know which ones?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ausalt? Sa ei tea. Sa õpid iga sõna paarina.
lines.id: Honestly? You don't. You learn each word as a pair.
lines.literal: honestly? you not know. you learn-you each word pair-as.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: See on nagu saksa keeles der, die, das.
lines.id: That's like der, die, das in German.
lines.literal: that is-it like German language-in der, die, das.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Täpselt nii. Ja hea uudis: omastav kannab kõiki teisi lõppe.
lines.id: Exactly. And the good news: the genitive carries all the other endings.
lines.literal: exactly so. and good news: genitive carries-it all-PARTITIVE other-PARTITIVE ending-PLURAL-PARTITIVE.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nii et kui ma tean "jala", siis ma tean ka "jalas" ja "jalast"?
lines.id: So if I know "jala", I also know "jalas" and "jalast"?
lines.literal: so that if I know-I "foot-GEN", then I know-I also "foot-in" and "foot-from"?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Just nimelt. Üks paar, kaksteist vormi.
lines.literal: precisely namely. one pair, twelve form-PARTITIVE.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Siis see ei olegi nii hull.
lines.id: Then this isn't so bad after all.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ei olegi. Lähme nüüd poodi — mul on leiba vaja.
lines.id: It isn't. Now let's go to the shop — I need bread.

lines.speaker: Kerli:

lines.id: Ha! That's already the next chapter.

notes: **Astmevaheldus** literally means "grade alternation" (in English, *consonant gradation*). The name is scary, the content is simple: some Estonian nouns and verbs have **two stems** — one strong, one weak — and which one appears depends on the ending attached.
**Omastav** is the Estonian name for the genitive ("of" / possessive) form. It is the most important form in all of Estonian, and the reason is in the next note.

⚠️ **The genitive is the stepping stone to almost every other form.** *Jalg* (foot) → *jala* (of the foot) → *jalas* (in the foot), *jalast* (from the foot), *jalale* (onto the foot), *jalaga* (with the foot). Ten endings attach to the same stem. So memorizing the pair isn't extra work — it's a shortcut.

**Maja jääb alati maja.** ("Maja always stays maja.") Not every word alternates. Words like *maja*, *sõna*, *päev*, *silm*, *kool* use the same stem for everything. A large part of your basic vocabulary turns out to be safe.

grammars.title: The ten gradation patterns you'll meet most often
body: This table is **not for memorizing**. Read it once, then come back to it when you meet a word that looks odd. What you really memorize is the word pairs, not the rules.
after: Notice that the direction of the weakening is always the same: **basic form strong, genitive weak**. Never the other way around. So if you see two shapes of one word, the "heavier" one is almost always the basic form.

Some words go further than just weakening a consonant — the vowels change too: *tuba → toa*, *nägu → näo*, *lugu → loo*, *jõgi → jõe*, *mägi → mäe*. This group is small but contains frequently used words, so memorize them straight away as pairs.

⚠️ There is also alternation in the opposite direction in some verbs — the basic form is weak and the form with an ending is strong. You don't need to think about it now; at A1 the noun pattern covers almost every need.

grammars.title: One pair, twelve forms
body: This is the real reason this unit exists. Take one word and see how many forms you get for free once you know its genitive.
after: Ten of the twelve rows use the same stem: **jala-**. You memorize one thing and get ten. That's a great deal, and it's why Estonian dictionaries always list the genitive next to the basic form.
The two rows that don't follow are the **basic form** and the **partitive** — both use the strong stem. For now just know that; both are covered in Unit 13.
Practical advice: **when you write a new word in your notebook, always write two forms.** *jalg – jala*, not just *jalg*. This habit cuts months of confusion down the road.

sections.title: Places in town — with their pairs

blocks.text: Look at the third column: **the "-s" ending attaches to the genitive**, not the basic form. *Apteek* → *apteegi* → *apteegi**s***. If you try attaching it to the basic form ("apteekis"), it comes out wrong. That's why the second column is there.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Three places that use -l, not -s
items: *turul* (at the market), *tänaval* (on the street), *väljakul* (on the square).
The reason is the same as the *-maa* rule in Unit 2: all three count as **open surfaces**, not enclosed rooms. You stand **on** the street, not inside it.
The same pattern applies to *põrandal* (on the floor), *laual* (on the table), *maal* (in the countryside), *tööl* (at work).
⚠️ *Tööl* is worth memorizing now: *Ma olen tööl* = "I'm at work". One of the sentences adult Estonians use most often.

blocks.text: These twenty words appear on almost every page of Estonian. Memorizing their pairs now saves an enormous amount of time later.

blocks.title: Words that never change — relax
items: *kino – kino*, *raadio – raadio*, *auto – auto*, *foto – foto* — almost all loanwords ending in a vowel are safe.
Words ending in *-mine*, *-us*, *-lane*, *-kond* are also safe: *õppimine*, *küsimus*, *eestlane*, *perekond*.
This is a large part of your vocabulary. Consonant gradation feels threatening because it hits the most frequently used words — not because it hits many words.

exercises.prompt: Write the genitive (omastav) of these words.
